Section 5.1 of Lock⁵ trades the dotplot for a curve: when a randomization
(or bootstrap) distribution is reasonably bell-shaped — which it usually is
for large samples — we stop simulating and approximate it with a **normal
distribution**. For a hypothesis test the approximating curve is
**$N(\text{null value},\ SE)$**: it is centered at the null value of the
parameter (the "if $H_0$ is true" world) and its spread is the standard
error taken from the randomization distribution. Rather than work with a
different curve for every problem, we standardize once and for all: the
**standardized test statistic**
$$z=\frac{\text{Sample Statistic}-\text{Null Parameter}}{SE}$$
measures how many standard errors the observed statistic sits from the null
value, and the **p-value is the tail area of the standard normal distribution
beyond $z$** — one tail for a one-sided alternative ($H_a\colon \mu > \mu_0$
or $\mu < \mu_0$), both tails for $H_a\colon \mu \ne \mu_0$. Below we compute
every area and p-value with the normal CDF (`scipy.stats.norm`), and, where
the exercise gives real data or exact counts, we verify the normal answer
against a randomization simulation (10000 simulated samples, seed 2026).
The exercises are from *Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data* (Lock⁵,
3rd ed., pp. 413–417): Skill Builders 5.1–5.6 find standard normal tail
areas; 5.7–5.12 compute $z$-statistics; 5.13–5.14 convert $z$ to p-values;
5.15–5.17 find areas in general $N(\mu,\sigma)$ curves; and the applied
exercises 5.18–5.33 carry out full tests, ending with Exercise 5.33 — a
cautionary tale about using the normal curve when the large-sample
conditions fail.

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path
_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_root / "_quarto.yml").exists():
    _root = _root.parent
os.chdir(_root)
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

def zstat(stat, null, se):
    """Standardized test statistic z = (statistic - null parameter) / SE."""
    return (stat - null) / se

def norm_p(z, tail):
    """p-value for a z-statistic read off a standard normal curve."""
    if tail == "right":
        return float(stats.norm.sf(z))
    if tail == "left":
        return float(stats.norm.cdf(z))
    return float(2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(z)))

def ztest_row(stat, null, se, tail, digits=4):
    """One-row summary: statistic, z-statistic, and normal-curve p-value."""
    z = zstat(stat, null, se)
    return pd.Series({"Statistic": round(float(stat), 4),
                      "Null value": round(float(null), 4),
                      "SE": se,
                      "z-statistic": round(float(z), 3),
                      "p-value (normal)": round(norm_p(z, tail), digits)})

def zcurve(z, tail, figsize=(6, 2.6)):
    """Standard normal curve with the p-value tail beyond z shaded."""
    x = np.linspace(-4.5, 4.5, 500)
    y = stats.norm.pdf(x)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    ax.plot(x, y, color="#4c72b0", lw=2)
    if tail == "right":
        mask = x >= z
    elif tail == "left":
        mask = x <= z
    else:
        mask = (x >= abs(z)) | (x <= -abs(z))
    if mask.any():
        ax.fill_between(x[mask], y[mask], color="#c44e52", alpha=0.65)
    ax.axvline(np.clip(z, -4.5, 4.5), color="black", lw=1)
    ax.set_xlabel("z")
    ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def rand_prop(n, p0, x, tail, reps=10000, seed=2026):
    """Randomization distribution for a single proportion: simulate `reps`
    samples of size n with success probability p0 (the null value) and record
    the sample proportion in each. Returns (proportions, p-value)."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    counts = r.binomial(n, p0, reps)
    props = counts / n
    if tail == "right":
        p = (counts >= x).mean()
    elif tail == "left":
        p = (counts <= x).mean()
    else:  # two-tailed: double the tail on the side of the observed statistic
        p = 2 * ((counts >= x).mean() if x / n >= p0 else (counts <= x).mean())
    return props, p

def shuffle_stats(pooled, n1, stat_fn, reps=10000, seed=2026):
    """Randomization distribution by shuffling group labels: permute `pooled`,
    give the first n1 values to group 1, and apply stat_fn(group1, group2)."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    pooled = np.asarray(pooled, float)
    out = np.empty(reps)
    for i in range(reps):
        perm = r.permutation(pooled)
        out[i] = stat_fn(perm[:n1], perm[n1:])
    return out

def tail_plot(boots, observed, tail, xlabel, null=0.0, bins=40, figsize=(6, 3)):
    """Histogram of a randomization distribution with the p-value tail shaded."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    sns.histplot(x=boots, bins=bins, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
    if tail == "right":
        mask = boots >= observed
    elif tail == "left":
        mask = boots <= observed
    else:
        mask = np.abs(boots - null) >= abs(observed - null)
    if mask.any():
        sns.histplot(x=boots[mask], bins=bins, ax=ax, color="#c44e52")
    ax.axvline(observed, color="black", lw=1.5)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel("Simulated statistics")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def p_row(label, stat, boots, tail, null=0.0, digits=4):
    """One-row summary: statistic and randomization p-value."""
    if tail == "right":
        p = (boots >= stat).mean()
    elif tail == "left":
        p = (boots <= stat).mean()
    else:
        p = (np.abs(boots - null) >= abs(stat - null)).mean()
    return pd.Series({label: round(float(stat), 4),
                      "Randomization p-value": round(float(p), digits),
                      "Simulated samples": len(boots)})
```

## Exercise 5.13

*(Skill Builder 3)* Find the p-value on a standard normal curve for each
standardized test statistic.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"(a) z = 0.84, right-tail": round(float(stats.norm.sf(0.84)), 4),
           "(b) z = -2.38, left-tail": round(float(stats.norm.cdf(-2.38)), 4),
           "(c) z = 2.25, two-tailed": round(float(2 * stats.norm.sf(2.25)), 4)}).to_string()
```

- **(a) p-value ≈ 0.2005** — the area to the right of 0.84.
- **(b) p-value ≈ 0.0087** — the area to the left of −2.38.
- **(c) p-value ≈ 0.0244** — *both* tails beyond ±2.25, i.e. twice the
  one-tailed area.

## Exercise 5.15

*(Skill Builder 4)* For a $N(60, 10)$ distribution find (a) the area to the
right of 65 and (b) the area to the left of 48.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: A N(60, 10) distribution with the area to the right of 65 and the area to the left of 48 shaded
x = np.linspace(22, 98, 600)
y = stats.norm.pdf(x, 60, 10)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.8))
ax.plot(x, y, color="#4c72b0", lw=2)
ax.fill_between(x[x >= 65], y[x >= 65], color="#c44e52", alpha=0.65)
ax.fill_between(x[x <= 48], y[x <= 48], color="#dd8452", alpha=0.65)
for v in (48, 65):
    ax.axvline(v, color="black", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("Value")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
pd.Series({"(a) Area right of 65": round(float(stats.norm.sf(65, 60, 10)), 4),
           "(b) Area left of 48": round(float(stats.norm.cdf(48, 60, 10)), 4)}).to_string()
```

- **(a) ≈ 0.3085** — 65 is only half a standard deviation above the mean.
- **(b) ≈ 0.1151** — 48 is 1.2 standard deviations below the mean.

## Exercise 5.18

**Effect of Organic Soybeans after 5 Days.** Testing
$H_0\colon p_o = p_c$ vs $H_a\colon p_o > p_c$ (proportions of fruit flies
alive after 5 days eating organic vs conventional soybeans);
$\hat p_o - \hat p_c = 0.90 - 0.84 = 0.06$, $SE = 0.021$, 5% level.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Standard normal curve with the right tail beyond z = 2.86 shaded
z = zstat(0.06, 0, 0.021)
zcurve(z, "right")
ztest_row(0.06, 0, 0.021, "right").to_string()
```

$z = 0.06/0.021 = 2.86$ and **p-value ≈ 0.0021**. Since $0.0021 < 0.05$ we
reject $H_0$: the difference in survival proportions is too large to
attribute to random chance, so the data provide convincing evidence that
fruit flies eating organic soybeans have a *higher* 5-day survival rate than
those eating conventional soybeans.

## Exercise 5.19

**Effect of Organic Bananas after 25 Days.** Same hypotheses;
$\hat p_o - \hat p_c = 0.42 - 0.40 = 0.02$, $SE = 0.031$, 5% level.

```{python}
#| echo: false
ztest_row(0.02, 0, 0.031, "right").to_string()
```

$z = 0.02/0.031 = 0.65$ and **p-value ≈ 0.259**. The p-value is much larger
than 0.05, so we do not reject $H_0$ — a 2-percentage-point advantage for
organic bananas is entirely plausible by random chance, and the data provide
no evidence that organic bananas improve 25-day survival.

## Exercise 5.21

**Effect of Organic Soybeans after 8 Days.** Same hypotheses;
$\hat p_o - \hat p_c = 0.79 - 0.32 = 0.47$, $SE = 0.031$, 5% level.

```{python}
#| echo: false
p = norm_p(zstat(0.47, 0, 0.031), "right")
pd.Series({"z-statistic": round(float(zstat(0.47, 0, 0.031)), 2),
           "p-value (normal)": float(f"{p:.2e}"),

```

$z = 0.47/0.031 = 15.16$ and **p-value ≈ $10^{-52}$ — effectively zero**. We
reject $H_0$ overwhelmingly: a 47-percentage-point survival advantage some
16 standard errors from the null is impossible to explain by chance, giving
very strong evidence that organic soybeans dramatically improve 8-day
survival.

## Exercise 5.22

**How Do You Get Your News?** In a 2010 random sample of $n = 1500$ US
adults, 66% said television was one of their main news sources. Test
whether more than 65% of all US adults used television as a main news
source: $H_0\colon p = 0.65$ vs $H_a\colon p > 0.65$, with randomization
$SE = 0.013$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Randomization distribution of sample proportions when p = 0.65, observed 0.66 shaded in the right tail
r = np.random.default_rng(2026)
boots = r.binomial(1500, 0.65, 10000) / 1500
tail_plot(boots, 0.66, "right", "Randomization sample proportions", bins=24)
pd.Series({"SE simulated": round(float(boots.std(ddof=1)), 4),
           "SE from book": 0.013}).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
ztest_row(0.66, 0.65, 0.013, "right").to_string()
```

$z = (0.66 - 0.65)/0.013 = 0.77$ and **p-value ≈ 0.221** — the simulation
above (randomizing 1500 coin flips with $p = 0.65$, giving
$SE \approx 0.012$) agrees: about 21% of randomization samples reach 0.66
or higher. Since $0.221 > 0.05$ we fail to reject $H_0$: a sample result of
66% is quite plausible when the true proportion is 65%, so the data provide
**no evidence** that more than 65% of all US adults used television as a
main news source.

## Exercise 5.23

**To Study Effectively, Test Yourself!** 118 students randomly split
between re-reading Swahili–English word pairs and self-quizzing; on the
final test a week later the recall proportions were 0.15 (reading) and 0.42
(self-quiz). Test $H_0\colon p_q = p_r$ vs $H_a\colon p_q > p_r$ with
$SE = 0.07$ for the difference in proportions.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Standard normal curve with the right tail beyond z = 3.86 shaded
z = zstat(0.42 - 0.15, 0, 0.07)
zcurve(z, "right")
ztest_row(0.42 - 0.15, 0, 0.07, "right").to_string()
```

$z = 0.27/0.07 = 3.86$ and **p-value ≈ 0.0001**. Since $0.0001 < 0.05$ we
reject $H_0$: if self-quizzing and re-reading were equally effective, a
sample advantage of 27 percentage points or more for the quizzers would
occur only about 1 time in 10000. The data provide strong evidence that
self-testing is the more effective study method.

## Exercise 5.24

**Penalty Shots in World Cup Soccer.** In 138 World Cup Finals penalty
shots (1982–1994), goalkeepers guessed the kick direction correctly only
41% of the time. Test $H_0\colon p = 0.5$ vs $H_a\colon p < 0.5$ (5%
level), with randomization $SE = 0.043$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Randomization distribution of sample proportions when p = 0.5 for 138 penalty shots, observed 0.41 shaded in the left tail
r = np.random.default_rng(2026)
boots = r.binomial(138, 0.5, 10000) / 138
tail_plot(boots, 0.41, "left", "Randomization sample proportions", bins=22)
pd.Series({"SE simulated": round(float(boots.std(ddof=1)), 4),
           "SE from book": 0.043}).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
ztest_row(0.41, 0.5, 0.043, "left").to_string()
```

$z = (0.41 - 0.5)/0.043 = -2.09$ and **p-value ≈ 0.018**; simulating 138
fair coin flips gives $SE \approx 0.042$ and about 1.6% of samples at or
below 0.41 — consistent. Since $0.018 < 0.05$ we reject $H_0$: goalkeepers
guess the correct direction significantly *less* than the 50% expected by
random chance — consistent with kickers placing shots where keepers are
not.

## Exercise 5.25

**Dogs Ignore an Unreliable Person.** Each of 26 dogs saw a reliable
experimenter and (on another trial) an unreliable one: 16 of 26 followed
the cue after reliable behavior, but only 7 of 26 after being misled. Test
$H_0\colon p_R = p_U$ vs $H_a\colon p_R \ne p_U$ with $SE = 0.138$ (5%
level).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Randomization distribution of the difference in proportions following the cue, reliable minus unreliable
follow = np.repeat([1.0, 0.0], [16 + 7, 52 - 23])
boots = shuffle_stats(follow, 26, lambda a, b: a.mean() - b.mean())
tail_plot(boots, 16 / 26 - 7 / 26, "two",
          "Difference in proportions following the cue (reliable - unreliable)")
p_row("Difference (reliable - unreliable)", 16 / 26 - 7 / 26, boots, "two").to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
ztest_row(16 / 26 - 7 / 26, 0, 0.138, "two").to_string()
```

Sample statistic: $\hat p_R - \hat p_U = 16/26 - 7/26 = 9/26 \approx 0.346$.
$z = 0.346/0.138 = 2.51$ and **p-value ≈ 0.012** (two-tailed); shuffling the
52 dogs into two groups of 26 above gives about the same p-value. Since
$0.012 < 0.05$ we reject $H_0$: dogs are significantly more likely to
follow a cue from a person who has just behaved reliably than from one who
just misled them.

## Exercise 5.26

**Exercise and Sex.** The `ExerciseHours` data give mean weekly exercise of
9.4 hours for 30 female and 12.4 hours for 20 male statistics students;
randomization of these data under $H_0\colon \mu_F = \mu_M$ gives
$SE = 2.38$. Test $H_a\colon \mu_F < \mu_M$ at the 5% level.

*Data:* `data/ch04/ExerciseHours.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/ExerciseHours.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
eh = pd.read_csv("data/ch04/ExerciseHours.csv")
fem = eh.loc[eh.Sex == "F", "Exercise"].dropna().to_numpy(float)
mal = eh.loc[eh.Sex == "M", "Exercise"].dropna().to_numpy(float)
pd.Series({"Mean hours, female": round(fem.mean(), 1),
           "Mean hours, male": round(mal.mean(), 1),
           "n female / male": f"{len(fem)} / {len(mal)}"}).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Randomization distribution of the difference in mean exercise hours, female minus male, from shuffling the ExerciseHours data
boots = shuffle_stats(np.concatenate([fem, mal]), len(fem),
                      lambda a, b: a.mean() - b.mean())
tail_plot(boots, fem.mean() - mal.mean(), "left",
          "Difference in mean exercise hours (female - male)")
p_row("Difference (female - male)", fem.mean() - mal.mean(), boots, "left").to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
ztest_row(fem.mean() - mal.mean(), 0, 2.38, "left").to_string()
```

$z = (9.4 - 12.4)/2.38 = -1.26$ and **p-value ≈ 0.104**. The shuffles of
the real data above reproduce the book's $SE \approx 2.4$ and give a
matching p-value. Since $0.104 > 0.05$ we fail to reject $H_0$: a mean
difference of 3 hours is not unusual when labels are assigned at random,
so the data do **not** show that female statistics students exercise less,
on average, than male statistics students.

## Exercise 5.27

**Smile Leniency.** In the Smiles experiment (Data 4.5), smiling subjects
were judged more leniently: $\bar x_s - \bar x_n = 4.91 - 4.12 = 0.79$, and
the randomization distribution of differences in means (Figure 5.12) is
bell-shaped with $SE \approx 0.393$. Test $H_0\colon \mu_s = \mu_n$ vs
$H_a\colon \mu_s > \mu_n$ using a normal distribution.

*Data:* `data/ch04/Smiles.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/Smiles.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
sm = pd.read_csv("data/ch04/Smiles.csv")
s = sm.loc[sm.Group == "smile", "Leniency"].dropna().to_numpy(float)
n = sm.loc[sm.Group == "neutral", "Leniency"].dropna().to_numpy(float)
pd.Series({"Mean leniency, smile": round(s.mean(), 2),
           "Mean leniency, neutral": round(n.mean(), 2),
           "Observed difference": round(s.mean() - n.mean(), 2)}).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Randomization distribution of the difference in mean leniency scores from shuffling the Smiles data, observed difference 0.79 marked
boots = shuffle_stats(np.concatenate([s, n]), len(s),
                      lambda a, b: a.mean() - b.mean())
tail_plot(boots, s.mean() - n.mean(), "right",
          "Difference in mean leniency (smile - neutral)")
p_row("Difference (smile - neutral)", s.mean() - n.mean(), boots, "right").to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
ztest_row(s.mean() - n.mean(), 0, 0.393, "right").to_string()
```

$z = 0.79/0.393 = 2.01$ and **p-value ≈ 0.022** — the area to the right of
$z = 2.01$ on a standard normal curve. Shuffling the real Smiles data above
reproduces Figure 5.12 ($SE \approx 0.39$, red dots beyond 0.79) and gives
the same p-value. **Interpretation:** if smiling had no effect on leniency,
a difference in sample means of 0.79 or more would occur in only about 2%
of random assignments — evidence at the 5% level that smiling increases the
leniency shown to students accused of cheating.

## Exercise 5.28

**How Often Do You Use Cash?** In an April 2012 survey of 1000 American
adults, 43% reported going an entire week without paying anything in cash.
Test $H_0\colon p = 0.40$ vs $H_a\colon p > 0.40$ (5% level), with
randomization $SE = 0.016$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Randomization distribution of sample proportions when p = 0.40, observed 0.43 shaded in the right tail
r = np.random.default_rng(2026)
boots = r.binomial(1000, 0.40, 10000) / 1000
tail_plot(boots, 0.43, "right", "Randomization sample proportions", bins=22)
pd.Series({"SE simulated": round(float(boots.std(ddof=1)), 4),
           "SE from book": 0.016}).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
ztest_row(0.43, 0.40, 0.016, "right").to_string()
```

$z = (0.43 - 0.40)/0.016 = 1.88$ and **p-value ≈ 0.030**; the simulation of
1000 coin flips with $p = 0.40$ gives $SE \approx 0.016$ and about 2.8% of
samples at 0.43 or above — consistent. Since $0.030 < 0.05$ we reject
$H_0$: the data provide evidence that more than 40% of all American adults
go a full week without paying cash.

## Exercise 5.29

**Incentives to Exercise: How Well Do They Work?** For 281 participants
assigned to walk 7000 steps a day over 100 days, the mean number of days
meeting the goal was 36.5 with $SE = 1.80$. Test $H_0\colon \mu = 35$ vs
$H_a\colon \mu > 35$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Standard normal curve with the right tail beyond z = 0.83 shaded
z = zstat(36.5, 35, 1.80)
zcurve(z, "right")
ztest_row(36.5, 35, 1.80, "right").to_string()
```

$z = (36.5 - 35)/1.80 = 0.83$ and **p-value ≈ 0.202**. Since $0.202 > 0.05$
we fail to reject $H_0$: a sample mean 1.5 days above 35 is well within
random-chance range, so the data provide no evidence that the mean number
of days meeting the goal exceeds 35.

## Exercise 5.30

**Incentives to Exercise: What Works Best?** In the same study, the three
non-loss incentive groups averaged 33.7 days meeting the goal, while the
group that *lost* money for missed days averaged 45.0 days. Test
$H_0\colon \mu_L = \mu_O$ vs $H_a\colon \mu_L \ne \mu_O$ with $SE = 4.14$
for the difference in means.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Standard normal curve with both tails beyond z = 2.73 shaded
z = zstat(45.0 - 33.7, 0, 4.14)
zcurve(z, "two")
ztest_row(45.0 - 33.7, 0, 4.14, "two").to_string()
```

$z = (45.0 - 33.7)/4.14 = 2.73$ and **p-value ≈ 0.006** (two-tailed). Since
$0.006 < 0.05$ we reject $H_0$: the difference of 11.3 days is too large to
attribute to random assignment chance, providing evidence that the
incentive structure matters — and specifically that people who stand to
*lose* money meet the step goal on many more days than those with other
incentives.

## Exercise 5.31

**Incentives for Quitting Smoking: Group or Individual?** Over 2000 smokers
trying to quit were randomly assigned to a group program (148 of 1080 still
abstaining at six months) or an individual program (120 of 990 successful).

- **(a)** $H_0\colon p_G = p_I$ vs $H_a\colon p_G \ne p_I$, where $p_G$ and
  $p_I$ are the proportions of all such smokers who would successfully quit
  with a group vs an individual program. Statistic:
  $\hat p_G - \hat p_I = 148/1080 - 120/990 \approx 0.137 - 0.121 = 0.016$.
- **(b) Randomization p-value:** shuffle the 2070 participants (268
  successes) into groups of 1080 and 990 (done below via the equivalent
  hypergeometric draw); two-tailed **p-value ≈ 0.29**.
- **(c)** The matching normal curve is $N(0,\ SE)$ with **mean 0** and
  **SE ≈ 0.0147** (the SD of the randomization differences): the normal
  p-value is about **0.28**.
- **(d)** Using the randomization SE, $z = 0.0158/0.0147 = 1.07$, giving
  **p-value ≈ 0.28** on the standard normal curve.
- **(e)** All three p-values (0.29, 0.28, 0.28) agree: a difference of
  0.016 is entirely typical of random assignment noise, so we fail to
  reject $H_0$ — the data provide **no evidence of a difference** in
  quitting success between group and individual programs.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Randomization distribution of the difference in quitting proportions, group minus individual, with both tails shaded
r = np.random.default_rng(2026)
g1 = r.hypergeometric(268, 2070 - 268, 1080, 10000)  # successes in the group arm after shuffling
boots = g1 / 1080 - (268 - g1) / 990
se = boots.std(ddof=1)
tail_plot(boots, 148 / 1080 - 120 / 990, "two",
          "Difference in quitting proportions (group - individual)")
pd.Series({"Statistic (pG - pI)": round(148 / 1080 - 120 / 990, 4),
           "(b) Randomization p-value": round(float((np.abs(boots) >= abs(148 / 1080 - 120 / 990)).mean()), 4),
           "(c) Randomization SE": round(float(se), 4),
           "(c) Normal p-value, N(0, SE)": round(float(2 * stats.norm.sf(abs((148 / 1080 - 120 / 990) / se))), 4),
           "(d) z-statistic": round(float((148 / 1080 - 120 / 990) / se), 3),
           "(d) Standard-normal p-value": round(float(2 * stats.norm.sf(abs((148 / 1080 - 120 / 990) / se))), 4)}).to_string()
```

## Exercise 5.32

**Incentives for Quitting Smoking: Do They Work?** With no incentive about
0.06 of quitters are still abstaining six months later. In the least
successful incentive group, 47 of 498 participants were abstaining.

- **(a)** $H_0\colon p = 0.06$ vs $H_a\colon p > 0.06$, where $p$ is the
  proportion who would successfully quit with even the smallest incentive.
  Statistic: $\hat p = 47/498 \approx 0.094$.
- **(b) Randomization p-value:** simulate 10000 samples of 498 people
  quitting with $p = 0.06$; **p-value ≈ 0.002**.
- **(c)** The matching normal curve is $N(0.06, SE)$ with **mean 0.06** and
  **SE ≈ 0.0106** (the SD of the simulated proportions,
  $\sqrt{0.06 \cdot 0.94/498}$): the p-value is
  $1 - \Phi((0.0944 - 0.06)/0.0106) \approx$ **0.0006**.
- **(d)** Using the randomization SE, $z = 0.0344/0.0106 = 3.23$, giving
  **p-value ≈ 0.0006** on the standard normal curve.
- **(e)** The p-values agree up to Monte Carlo wobble (the simulation
  counts discrete successes): all are far below 0.05, so we reject $H_0$ —
  strong evidence that even the smallest incentive raises six-month
  abstinence above the 0.06 obtained with no incentive at all.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Randomization distribution of the abstinence proportion when p = 0.06 for 498 smokers, observed 0.094 shaded in the right tail
r = np.random.default_rng(2026)
boots = r.binomial(498, 0.06, 10000) / 498
se = boots.std(ddof=1)
tail_plot(boots, 47 / 498, "right", "Randomization sample proportions", bins=24)
pd.Series({"Statistic": round(47 / 498, 4),
           "(b) Randomization p-value": round(float((boots >= 47 / 498).mean()), 4),
           "(c) Randomization SE": round(float(se), 4),
           "(c) Normal p-value, N(0.06, SE)": round(float(stats.norm.sf((47 / 498 - 0.06) / se)), 5),
           "(d) z-statistic": round(float((47 / 498 - 0.06) / se), 3),
           "(d) Standard-normal p-value": round(float(stats.norm.sf((47 / 498 - 0.06) / se)), 5)}).to_string()
```

## Exercise 5.33

**Lucky Numbers.** If lottery digits are chosen at random the last digit is
7 with probability $p = 0.10$; among $n = 20$ people asked for a three-digit
number, four ended in 7, so $\hat p = 0.20$. Figure 5.13 shows the
randomization distribution of proportions for 5000 simulated samples under
$H_0\colon p = 0.10$: mean 0.101, SD 0.067, right-tail area (beyond 0.200)
equal to 0.137.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Our randomization distribution for Exercise 5.33 with the N(0.101, 0.067) normal approximation overlaid, observed 0.20 marked
sims = np.random.default_rng(2026).binomial(20, 0.10, 10000) / 20
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
sns.histplot(x=sims, bins=np.arange(-0.025, 0.475, 0.05), ax=ax,
             color="#4c72b0", stat="density")
xg = np.linspace(-0.05, 0.45, 400)
ax.plot(xg, stats.norm.pdf(xg, 0.101, 0.067), color="black", lw=2)
ax.axvline(0.20, color="#c44e52", lw=1.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Randomization sample proportions")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
pd.Series({"Simulated mean": round(float(sims.mean()), 3),
           "Simulated SD": round(float(sims.std(ddof=1)), 3),
           "Right-tail p, simulation": round(float((sims >= 0.20).mean()), 3),
           "(a) z-statistic": round(float(zstat(0.20, 0.101, 0.067)), 2),
           "(b) p-value, normal": round(float(stats.norm.sf(zstat(0.20, 0.101, 0.067))), 4)}).to_string()
```

- **(a)** Using the sample proportion $\hat p = 0.20$ and the standard
  error from the randomization distribution:
  $$z=\frac{0.20-0.101}{0.067}\approx 1.48$$
- **(b)** The upper-tail area beyond $z = 1.48$ on a standard normal curve
  is **p-value ≈ 0.070**.
- **(c)** The randomization distribution gives a right-tail p-value of
  **0.137** — roughly double the normal answer (our own 10000-sample
  simulation above reproduces the figure: mean 0.100, SD 0.068, right tail
  0.135). The discrepancy arises because the large-sample conditions fail
  badly here: with $n = 20$ and $p_0 = 0.10$, a sample averages only
  $np_0 = 2$ successes, so the randomization distribution takes just the
  few values $0, 0.05, \ldots, 0.45$ — highly discrete and visibly
  right-skewed (see the tall spikes and the poor normal fit above). A bell
  curve is simply not a good model for this distribution, and the normal
  p-value understates how often $\hat p \ge 0.20$ occurs by chance. This is
  the section's built-in warning: use the normal approximation only when
  the sample is large enough for the randomization distribution to be
  reasonably normal.

:::
